new strength to bring happiness and joy to others. And in
so far as we see that we can be a source of blessing to others,
we may justifiably feel that we are something of value in
ourselves. It then becomes clear to us that it is not what we
have planned and intentionally done which confers the
richest content and meaning on our lives, but rather what
we have gratefully received and faithfully preserved as a gift,
and that the greatest of these gifts bestowed on us is love.
We come to see that in the fellowship of love and trust,
whose secret network mysteriously interpenetrates the world
of the tangible and of purposeful organization, our true
essential life is rooted.
"Behold, I stand at the door and knock." This finally
applies to the word of Holy Scripture, which summons us to
vigilance and readiness. This word is not faded or remote;
old as it is, it speaks to us ever anew. It strikes home to the
heart of our daily life as the word which sounds from
another world. It vibrates essentially in the very sound of our
church bells, so different from all the other sounds which
beat upon our ears—an alien mysterious sound at the heart
of our so familiar world. And it would be a sad day for us if
ever the music of church bells were to become silent in our
villages and towns. For it is this music which calls us away
from the world of visible things, the world of our scheming
and talking, inviting us to gather ourselves together to hear
the word of God which resounds from the invisible world of
eternity: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if any one
hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him
and eat with him, and he with me." Who is this "I" which
calls us thus? It is eternity—the eternity which addresses us
also in the messengers it sends. Yet here it speaks with a
clearer voice, lending to those other messages their full
meaning. For here God speaks to us through His word, in
